strings.name: Anselm Kiefer
strings.summary: Anselm Kiefer is a German artist long based in France. His paintings, sculptures, artist’s books and large installations explore German history, Holocaust memory, poetry and myth. Materials such as lead and straw connect images, writing and physical transformation. His early use of Nazi symbols questioned suppressed history and also provoked interpretive controversy.
strings.coverageNote: Reviewed through November 17, 2026. Critical historical context is retained: depicting Nazi symbols is not treated as political endorsement. Creation, exhibition, expansion and future schedules are distinguished; an exhibition does not establish the artist’s attendance.
strings.influence.rationale: Uses large paintings and installations to address war memory, myth and materials, advancing discussion of German history and cultural responsibility in contemporary art.
strings.facts.f1.label: Artistic training
strings.facts.f1.value: Studied law and Romance languages before art training in Freiburg and Karlsruhe under Peter Dreher and Horst Antes. Contact with Beuys is not presented as a formal degree under him.
strings.facts.f2.label: Poetry and materials
strings.facts.f2.value: The museum’s 1981 Thy Golden Hair Margarethe uses acrylic, emulsion, charcoal and straw on burlap, drawing on Paul Celan’s Death Fugue.
strings.highlights.h1.title: Historical memory and self-questioning
strings.highlights.h1.text: Uses German culture, wartime ruins and literary imagery to question postwar identity and historical responsibility, retaining complexity and disputed interpretations.
strings.highlights.h2.title: From image to space
strings.highlights.h2.text: Incorporates lead books, concrete, plants and architectural structures, connecting painting, sculpture and studio environments.
strings.timeline.t1.title: Barcelona exhibition opens
strings.timeline.t1.text: La Pedrera presents The Secret Life of Plants, centered on the Grothe Collection; scheduled through January 24, 2027, it had not ended at the cutoff.
strings.timeline.t2.title: La Ribaute opens to the public
strings.timeline.t2.text: The foundation opens the Barjac studio estate in France through seasonal guided tours, not unrestricted year-round access.
strings.timeline.t3.title: Receives Peace Prize of the German Book Trade
strings.timeline.t3.text: Awarded by the German Publishers and Booksellers Association, with a ceremony at Frankfurt’s St. Paul’s Church; not the Nobel Peace Prize.
strings.timeline.t4.title: The Seven Heavenly Palaces goes on permanent display
strings.timeline.t4.text: Pirelli HangarBicocca in Milan presents seven towers; five paintings added in 2015 form The Seven Heavenly Palaces 2004–2015.
strings.timeline.t5.title: Receives Praemium Imperiale
strings.timeline.t5.text: The Japan Art Association awards the painting prize, distinct from the sculpture category.
strings.timeline.t6.title: Moves to Barjac, France
strings.timeline.t6.text: According to the foundation’s chronology, leaves Germany to live and work at a former silk factory, later developed into La Ribaute.
strings.timeline.t7.title: Exhibits in the West German pavilion in Venice
strings.timeline.t7.text: Represents the Federal Republic alongside Georg Baselitz; the two artists and the historical context remain distinct.
strings.timeline.t8.title: Undertakes Occupations actions
strings.timeline.t8.text: Reenacts the Nazi salute at European locations and records it to provoke reflection on war memory and German identity; the controversial work requires its historical context.
